source.title: Isolated Mononeuropathy From Rucksack Palsy: A Case Series

extraction_metadata.source_type_note: This is a three-case series with narrative review. Secondary literature results are tagged secondary_reported_result and are not represented as results generated by this case series.

atoms.canonical_statement: The primary aim was to describe the clinical patterns of isolated spinal accessory and long thoracic mononeuropathies associated with rucksack palsy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The primary aim of this case series is to introduce the clinical patterns of isolated mononeuropathies involving the SAN and the LTN secondary to rucksack palsy.

atoms.canonical_statement: Secondary aims were to illustrate the need for education about improper rucksack use and to highlight rucksack safety features.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The secondary aims include illustrating the need for education on the risks of improper rucksack use and highlighting the safety features to improve the modern rucksack.

atoms.canonical_statement: The article presents three military cases of rucksack-associated mononeuropathy and reviews factors related to rucksack construction, components, fitting, use, and education.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Three cases of mononeuropathy secondary to rucksack use in military personnel are presented, including injuries to the long thoracic and spinal accessory nerves.

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 1 was a 29-year-old active duty male soldier.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A 29-year-old active duty male soldier presented with generalized left shoulder and periscapular pain

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: during a period in which he frequently wore body armor and carried rucksacks for his military occupation.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: generalized left shoulder and periscapular pain, as well as weakness with shrugging exercises. His symptoms began insidiously five years prior

exposures.details: Military occupational use over the period preceding symptoms

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 1 examination showed left upper trapezius atrophy and lateral scapular winging without other neurologic findings.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: His physical examination revealed left upper trapezius atrophy and left-sided lateral scapular winging on provocative testing, with no other neurologic findings.

population.label: Case 1: 29-year-old active duty male soldier

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 1 nerve conduction testing showed a markedly reduced left spinal accessory nerve compound motor action potential relative to the contralateral side.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: nerve conduction study (NCS) demonstrated markedly reduced left SAN compound motor action potential relative to the contralateral side.

population.label: Case 1: 29-year-old active duty male soldier

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 1 needle EMG showed mildly reduced left trapezius recruitment while the serratus anterior was normal.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Needle electromyography (EMG) of the left trapezius demonstrated mildly reduced recruitment while the serratus anterior was normal.

population.label: Case 1: 29-year-old active duty male soldier

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors diagnosed Case 1 with chronic incomplete left spinal accessory neuropathy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A diagnosis of chronic, incomplete, left spinal accessory neuropathy was made.

population.label: Case 1: 29-year-old active duty male soldier

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 1 underwent ultrasound-guided hydrodissection of the left spinal accessory nerve.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The patient subsequently underwent ultrasound-guided hydrodissection of the left SAN with good pain relief.

population.label: Case 1: 29-year-old active duty male soldier

atoms.canonical_statement: After hydrodissection, Case 1 had good pain relief, continued his military occupation, and had no later documented encounters for left shoulder symptoms.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: with good pain relief. He has since continued with his military occupation, with no documented encounters for left shoulder symptoms thereafter.

population.label: Case 1: 29-year-old active duty male soldier

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 2 was a 21-year-old U.S. Naval Academy male midshipman.

population.label: Case 2: 21-year-old U.S. Naval Academy male midshipman

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: His symptoms began following a 13-mile ruck march while training overseas. He reported using an older model rucksack with an internal frame, which was loaded with 65 pounds.

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 2 presented with right medial scapular winging, push-up weakness, and mild nonneuropathic shoulder pain.

concept.text: 13-mile ruck march with an older internal-frame rucksack loaded to 65 pounds

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 2 electrodiagnostic testing showed spontaneous activity in the right serratus anterior, no findings of right brachial plexopathy, and normal right trapezius and rhomboid EMG.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A subsequent electrodiagnostic study revealed spontaneous activity in right serratus anterior, no findings of right brachial plexopathy, and a normal right trapezius and rhomboid on EMG.

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 3 was a 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger initially presented with a three-month history of left shoulder weakness

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 3 developed left shoulder weakness after prolonged rucksack marches during a field training course.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: left shoulder weakness following prolonged rucksack marches at a field training course.

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

concept.text: prolonged rucksack marches during a field training course

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 3 could not actively flex or abduct the left shoulder beyond 90 degrees, had preserved passive range of motion, and showed medial scapular winging with forward flexion and wall push-up.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: His examination was notable for inability to actively flex or abduct his left shoulder beyond 90 degrees. Passive range of motion was preserved. There was medial scapular winging with forward shoulder flexion and wall push-up

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: Case 3 EMG showed abnormal spontaneous activity and reduced recruitment in the left serratus anterior, and NCS showed a markedly reduced left long thoracic nerve compound motor action potential relative to the contralateral side.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: EMG of the left serratus anterior revealed abnormal spontaneous activity and reduced motor unit recruitment. NCS demonstrated markedly reduced left LTN compound motor action potential relative to the contralateral side.

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors diagnosed Case 3 with incomplete left long thoracic neuropathy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A diagnosis of left, incomplete long thoracic neuropathy was made.

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: At nine months, follow-up EMG in Case 3 showed serratus anterior reinnervation and normalization of motor unit recruitment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Follow-up EMG of the left serratus anterior nine months later showed evidence of reinnervation and normalization of his motor unit recruitment pattern.

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: At eight months after injury, Case 3 could perform more than 53 push-ups.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: At eight months postinjury, he was able to perform over 53 push-ups.

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: By 17 months, Case 3 had returned to full unrestricted military duty but still had difficulty with weighted overhead presses.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: By 17 months, he had returned to full military duty without restrictions, although he remained unable to effectively do weighted overhead presses

population.label: Case 3: 25-year-old active-duty male U.S. Army Ranger

atoms.canonical_statement: Table I summarizes one left spinal accessory neuropathy and two long thoracic neuropathies, with lateral winging in Case 1 and medial winging in Cases 2 and 3.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Table summarizing clinical features, NCS, EMG, and diagnosis for the three cases presented.

atoms.canonical_statement: Table II lists prolonged shoulder load, improper strap positioning or donning, older or frameless rucksacks, heavy loads, and thin body habitus as risk factors summarized by the authors.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Risk Factors 1. Prolonged load on shoulder 2. Improper rucksack strap positioning and improper donning maneuvers 3. Older model rucksacks and rucksacks without frames 4. Heavy load carries 5. Thin body habitus

atoms.canonical_statement: Table II summarizes management as stopping provocative activity, allowing time for neuropraxic recovery, physical therapy for biomechanics, and selective surgical neurolysis for severe cases.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Management 1. Cessation of provocative activities 2. As neuropraxic injuries may take week or months to fully resolve, a trial of time is indicated 3. Physical therapy aimed at restoring biomechanics

atoms.canonical_statement: The introduction reports prior estimates of rucksack palsy incidence among service members of 29.7 to 53.7 per 100,000 per year and states that the true figures are unknown.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the incidence of rucksack palsy among service members has been estimated to be between 29.7 and 53.7 per 100,000 (0.0297%–0.0537%) military individuals each year, although the true figures are unknown.

atoms.canonical_statement: The discussion reports a cited biomechanical study in which anatomically modeled straps produced four times lower subclavian artery strain and 50% lower skin stress than a standard strap.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: anatomically modeled straps produced four times lower strain on the subclavian artery and 50% lower skin stresses compared with the standard strap.

atoms.canonical_statement: The discussion reports a cited 1987 study with yearly rucksack paralysis incidences of 0.157 per 1000 soldiers using framed packs and 1.17 per 1000 using packs without frames.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: The incidence of rucksack paralysis was calculated to be 0.157 per 1000 soldiers (0.0157%) using a pack with a frame and 1.17 per 1000 soldiers (0.117%) using a pack without a frame each year.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that most conclusions about the superiority of modern rucksacks are anecdotal.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Although most of these modern packs exhibit hip belts, modified frames, and larger shoulder straps, most of the conclusions on superiority are anecdotal.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that trends in rucksack palsy incidence are difficult to define because military units train and operate under different conditions and loads.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: the trend for incidence of rucksack palsy is difficult to define, especially as different units are often training and operating under different conditions and loads.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that more research is needed to determine rucksack design factors that may prevent injury.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: More research is needed to determine other factors in rucksack design that may prevent injury.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors conclude that isolated mononeuropathy from rucksack use is under-recognized and most commonly affects the long thoracic and spinal accessory nerves.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Isolated mononeuropathy secondary to rucksack use is an under-recognized condition and most commonly affects the LTN and SAN.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors conclude that a history of rucksack use with scapular winging should prompt further evaluation, including electrodiagnostic examination.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A history of rucksack use in association with scapular winging should warrant further evaluation, including electrodiagnostic examination.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that education of active duty soldiers about rucksack palsy may prevent many cases and that provider awareness may improve recognition and treatment.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: With proper education for active duty soldiers in operational and training environments, many cases of rucksack palsy may be prevented.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that more research is needed to determine which modern rucksack is most effective for preventing rucksack palsy.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: More research is needed to conclude which modern rucksack is most effective in preventing rucksack palsy.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors state that rucksack modernization is effective only when designs account for intrinsic and extrinsic factors affecting the warfighter.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Modernizations, however, are only effective if designs consider intrinsic and extrinsic factors affecting the warfighter.
